extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, clinicians, and policymakers interested in COVID-19 treatments and misinformation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize standards, evidence, regulatory positions, ethical issues, and misinformation indicators relating to ivermectin's use during the COVID-19 pandemic. Intended to capture what counts as valid evidence, appropriate clinical use, and red flags for poor science or advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and guideline recommendations against use for COVID-19
rubrics_metrics.description: The World Health Organization (WHO), the European Medicines Agency (EMA), the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) all do not advise using ivermectin in an attempt to treat or prevent COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EMA: "the available data do not support its use for COVID‑19 outside well-designed clinical trials"; WHO: ivermectin should not be used to treat COVID-19 except in a clinical trial; FDA: not approved for any viral illness. These agency statements are the baseline policy/clinical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological plausibility / dose requirement (in vitro vs clinical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some in vitro studies showed ivermectin inhibits SARS‑CoV‑2 replication (IC50 of 2.2–2.8 μM), but doses much higher than the maximum approved or safely achievable in humans would be required for an antiviral effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laboratory antiviral effects do not imply clinical utility if required concentrations cannot be safely achieved in humans. Mechanism (inhibition of importin α/β1-mediated nuclear transport) suggests host-process suppression and toxicity concerns; several drugs with similar mechanisms failed clinically due to systemic toxicity and narrow therapeutic windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence quality and methodological limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many studies on ivermectin for COVID‑19 have serious methodological limitations, resulting in very low evidence certainty; several publications supporting efficacy were retracted due to errors, unverifiable data, ethical concerns, or suspected data falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of small, poorly designed, non-randomized, open-label, or unverifiable studies; retractions and data-fraud materially undermine pooled estimates. High risk of bias in primary studies makes meta-analyses unreliable if they include flawed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for randomized controlled trials and large-scale evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To resolve uncertainties from small or poor-quality studies, large-scale randomized controlled trials (e.g., ACTIV-6) were undertaken; ACTIV-6 (published October 2022) found ivermectin was not effective as a COVID‑19 treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomized, adequately powered, well-conducted clinical trials are the appropriate standard to establish (or refute) efficacy. Reliance on observational studies or poor-quality trials is insufficient for treatment recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and informed consent in treatment interventions and research
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution of ivermectin as a public-health intervention and publication of the observed results without informed consent (Mexico City example) was judged unethical; such studies/papers have been withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-subjects research and programmatic interventions require informed consent and ethical oversight. Failure to obtain informed consent can justify retraction/withdrawal and is a public-harm risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate clinical use: treatment of strongyloidiasis in corticosteroid recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: WHO, ECDC, PHAC and CDC recommend presumptive treatment for strongyloidiasis with ivermectin in people at high or moderate risk of Strongyloides stercoralis infection before or in conjunction with corticosteroids for COVID‑19, to prevent hyperinfection syndrome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a specific, parasitological indication for ivermectin (management of strongyloidiasis), not an indication for treating COVID‑19 itself. Use in this context is to prevent steroid-triggered strongyloides hyperinfection, not to treat SARS‑CoV‑2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk stratification for presumptive strongyloidiasis treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: People born, resident in, or with long-term travel to certain regions are classified as high or moderate risk for strongyloidiasis: high risk — Southeast Asia, Oceania, sub‑Saharan Africa, South America, Caribbean; moderate risk — Central America, Eastern Europe, the Mediterranean, Mexico, Middle East, North Africa, Indian subcontinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumptive ivermectin treatment prior to corticosteroids is recommended based on these geographic risk categories. Clinical decision-making should use these stratifications to target antiparasitic therapy appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory authorizations and off‑label/compassionate use are provisional and variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some governments granted official approval, off‑label use, or compassionate-use exemptions for ivermectin (e.g., Czech Republic, Slovakia, Mexico, Peru [later rescinded], India [later rescinded], Philippines); some compassionate programs were later revoked due to lack of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of an authorization or a local program does not equate to established efficacy; such decisions may rely on limited/preliminary evidence and can be reversed as higher-quality data arrive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use veterinary ivermectin formulations for humans
rubrics_metrics.description: People desperate to use ivermectin without a prescription took veterinary preparations (horse dewormer), causing shortages and cases of poisoning; the FDA and CDC issued warnings (FDA tweet: "You are not a horse. You are not a cow. Seriously, y'all. Stop it").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veterinary formulations are not approved for human use; dosing, formulation, and contaminants differ and can cause severe harm. Poison-control calls and hospitalizations increased when people self‑medicated with veterinary products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags in meta-analysis and evidence synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading meta‑analysis websites and publications violated basic norms: inclusion of studies with widely different dosages, open‑label designs, poor or absent control groups, unpublished ad‑hoc trials that did not undergo peer review, and incompatible outcome measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing systematic reviews/meta-analyses, check for consistent dosages, study designs, control-group adequacy, peer‑review status, and harmonized outcome measures; heterogeneity and inclusion of low‑quality or non‑verifiable trials can produce spurious findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, conflicts of interest, and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where researchers or clinicians promoted ivermectin while having undisclosed commercial interests (e.g., filing patents for related combinations) raised concerns about undisclosed conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full disclosure of financial interests, patents, and other COIs is required for credible research and public statements; undisclosed COIs undermine trust and may bias recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and indicators of organized misinformation and advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ivermectin advocacy/misinformation spread via social media influencers, anonymous websites, misleading meta‑analysis sites, fake endorsements, and networks selling drugs to targeted audiences (e.g., right‑wing or vaccine‑hesitant groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags include anonymous site ownership, multiple domains redirecting to the same content, reused servers associated with past misinformation, sensational/misleading graphics, fabricated endorsements, and coordinated marketing to particular demographics. These indicate low credibility and high risk of misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and civil‑rights implications of non‑consensual prescribing
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples exist of ivermectin being prescribed to prisoners without consent, resulting in legal action and settlements (e.g., Washington County Detention Center, Arkansas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical ethics and law protect against non-consensual medical experimentation or treatment; failure to obtain consent can lead to litigation, compensation, and professional censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public‑health surveillance signals (poison control and prescribing patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharp rises in poison-control center calls and changes in prescribing patterns (including political‑pattern associations) were observed during the ivermectin surge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surges in poison-control calls, hospitalizations, stock shortages, and geographically/politically patterned prescribing can signal misuse driven by misinformation and warrant public-health alerts and targeted communication.
